resources.string: Passes only appear if logging is set to Everything. Otherwise they were never recorded in the first place.
The log is not readable yet. It lives in credential-encrypted storage, which only exists after the first unlock since boot.
The ring buffer could not be read, so anything logged since this screen last refreshed is missing here. Diagnostics has the reason.
Only the end of this name was stored. The matched rule is a suffix, so what is shown is the part that matched: the beginning of the name is missing, not blocked.

Un-blocking takes effect on the resolver\'s very next lookup: a blocked answer is never put in the system DNS cache, so there is nothing stale of ours to clear. What Nullroute cannot reach is the cache inside the app itself. OkHttp, Chromium and the Java resolver each remember a failed lookup for a while, and Android does not let this app flush them. That is why force stop is offered here.
It is not live yet. An allow rule only takes effect once the index has been recompiled.
The rule could not be written to allow.txt. Diagnostics has the storage state.
Compiling. This uses the lists already downloaded and does not need the network.
%1$s is exempt from filtering as of the resolver\'s next lookup.
Nullroute will not exempt itself. The liveness probe resolves from this process, so an exemption here would make the status card report a healthy filter as dead.
Per-app policy cannot be changed: control.bin is not mapped. Diagnostics has the reason.
This uid belongs to no installed package, so there is nothing to exempt. Usually it is an app that was uninstalled after the record was written.
The app closes immediately and loses anything unsaved. It starts again the next time you open it, with its in-process DNS caches empty, which is the point.
This build cannot force stop apps: FORCE_STOP_PACKAGES is not granted. Close the app from Recents instead.
Nullroute will not force stop itself.
This changes how an app experiences a block. It does not change what gets blocked.
Byte-identical to a real NXDOMAIN. The app makes no connection attempt and spends no battery on one. The default, and the right answer almost everywhere.
The name exists but has no address. Some apps treat NXDOMAIN as a hard error or a retry loop and treat this as an ordinary empty result. Worth trying when one of them misbehaves.

Not \"nowhere\". Linux rewrites a connection to 0.0.0.0 into a connection to 127.0.0.1, so the app connects to itself and whatever it is listening on answers, which can look exactly like the ad server replied. It also costs a socket and a timeout per request. An escape hatch for one stubborn app, never a default.
Apps will connect to themselves instead of failing. Use it to work around one app that breaks on NXDOMAIN, then put it back.
Saved, but not live: control.bin is not mapped, so the resolver is still using its previous setting. Diagnostics has the reason.
Once a day, when the battery is not low.
Off allows a list download on mobile data. Lists are fetched conditionally, so an unchanged list costs one request.
The daily job is registered with the system scheduler.
No update job is registered, so nothing will update on its own.
Update started. The Update screen shows what it is doing.

Nullroute filters names. An ad served from the same domain as the content around it has no separate name to refuse, so nothing at this layer blocks it, and an app that resolves its own names, Chrome included, is only filtered when Deep mode is on.

The query log is the one thing Nullroute keeps in credential-encrypted storage. Until you unlock the device after a reboot nothing can read it, Nullroute included, so a phone that is off or locked holds no readable browsing history. Lookups made in that window are never stored, and the log says so rather than quietly looking complete.
This is set at the source. Turning it off stops the resolver writing records, not merely this app storing them, and it deletes what is already stored.
Shortening this deletes anything already older, immediately. Records are also capped at %1$d rows, oldest dropped first.
The log database is not readable right now, for the reason above.
Nothing was old enough or over the cap.
Every stored record goes. This cannot be undone, and it does not change what is logged from now on.

Every app on this device asks the system resolver for names, and Nullroute answers the blocked ones there. No VPN slot is taken, nothing proxies your traffic, and there is no service to keep alive: the filter is already inside the process that was going to answer anyway.

An ad served from the same domain as the content around it has no separate name to refuse, so it is not blocked. That is true of every DNS-based blocker, this one included. Chrome and some other apps resolve names themselves and bypass the system resolver entirely; they are only filtered if you turn on Deep mode, which does take the VPN slot. And blocking by name cannot see inside a connection, so Nullroute counts requests refused, never ads removed from a page.
When something breaks, fix it in two taps

If an app starts failing, Nullroute notices the burst of blocked lookups coming from whatever you are using and offers to exempt it. In the log you can allow a single domain or exempt the whole app. Un-blocking is instant at the resolver, but apps cache their own failures, so the app may need to be reopened. Force stop sits next to the button for exactly that reason.
The log stays on the device

Logging starts at blocked lookups only, kept for seven days, in storage that is unreadable until you unlock the phone. Nothing is uploaded, there is no account, and updating fetches public blocklists without sending anything about you. You can turn logging off completely, and off means the resolver stops writing records at all.
Pausing stops the resolver filter. The roughly 2,000 domains in the built-in hosts list keep being blocked either way: pause is not off.
One tap further away from switching protection off by accident, and safer on a lock screen other people can reach.
Opens the app to confirm instead of pausing straight from the shade.
The tile label shows the last measured state rather than a live one, because a Quick Settings tile has no time to run a probe. Opening the app re-measures.
